copy.headline: Government's budget raises defence spending and cuts taxes

extended.text: The government presented its finance bill for 2027, the state's budget, on Friday. It would raise defence spending to 3.5 per cent of GDP by 2030 and set aside 10.1 billion kroner that year for tax cuts, among them scrapping the middle-bracket and top-top taxes and lowering corporate tax.

Unlike recent budgets, this one needs financing. Students living at home lose SU, the state study grant; fewer people will qualify for the seniorpension for worn-out workers; cruise ships face a levy; and state administration is to be cut.

'The Danish economy is in top form,' said Peter Hummelgaard, the finance minister. Pia Olsen Dyhr, the economy minister, called the grant cut 'a compromise'. Her party, SF, a left-wing party, has defended the grant.

The government must now find a majority in the Folketing, Denmark's parliament, and holds back 500 million kroner a year for other parties' wishes. Enhedslisten, a far-left party, and Alternativet, a green party, are expected to join the deal, and criticism of the grant cut has already come from them.

copy.headline: Funen firm confirms its access was used to leak 8.8 million Danish ID numbers

standard.text: Pays ApS, a software firm in Odense, on Funen, confirmed on Friday that its legal access to the CPR register had been misused in the leak of 8.8 million CPR numbers, Denmark's personal identification numbers. The firm had two employees in July. The intruder had access for 21 days and 17 hours in all, starting on 10 September.

Politiken found that at least three of the firm's profiles, including its administrator account, used the password '123456'. 'There is in reality no security, it is an open door,' Jens Myrup Pedersen, a professor of electrical and computer engineering at Aarhus University, told the paper.

copy.headline: Parties threaten to veto the government's cut to early retirement for worn-out workers

standard.text: Venstre, a liberal party, says it will veto the government's plan to tighten access to the seniorpension, an early-retirement scheme for worn-out workers. All parties to the 2019 agreement behind it must agree to changes within a parliamentary term.

The plan, in the government's budget proposal, would save 1.5 billion kroner up to 2030 by judging applicants' capacity to work in any job, not just their latest. The money would raise the monthly Arne-pension, another early-pension scheme, by 3,095 kroner from 1 January 2027.
Dansk Folkeparti, a nationalist party, also refuses. A deal taking effect after the next election would need Enhedslisten, a far-left party backing the government, and it says no too.

short.text: Venstre, a liberal party, says it will veto the government's plan to tighten access to the seniorpension, an early-retirement scheme for worn-out workers, which would save 1.5 billion kroner up to 2030. Dansk Folkeparti, a nationalist party, and Enhedslisten, a far-left party backing the government, also refuse.

copy.deck: Two parties to the deal behind the scheme refuse; the 1.5 billion kroner saved would fund a rise in another early pension.

copy.headline: Defence minister calls Russian TV report on flare incident misinformation

standard.text: Jeppe Bruus, the defence minister, calls a Russian state-television report on the frigate that fired flares at a Danish military helicopter a 'misinformation campaign' meant to 'sow distrust of the Danish authorities'. The Defence Command says part of the footage was not filmed on the day.

The report, shown on Thursday, says the helicopter 'entered the ship's safety zone' and does not show the firing. On 14 September the Soobrazitelny fired two flares without warning in international waters off Gedser, a town in southern Denmark; one passed 10 to 15 metres from the helicopter.
Politiken writes that the report turns the firing into a hero's story.

short.text: Jeppe Bruus, the defence minister, calls a Russian state-television report a 'misinformation campaign'. It covers the frigate that fired two flares at a Danish military helicopter off Gedser, a town in southern Denmark, on 14 September; the Defence Command says part of the footage was not filmed that day.

copy.headline: Justice minister orders a review of the police investigation into a girl's kidnapping

standard.text: Nicolai Wammen, the justice minister, will set up a special group of experienced investigators to review the police investigation in the Kirkerup case, the kidnapping of a 13-year-old girl in 2023. Investigators from NSK, the National Unit for Special Crime, will take part. Wammen announced the review on Friday in a statement to the Folketing, Denmark's parliament, after a police report raised new questions about the investigation.

The report shows that 'on some of the criticisms raised, the police cannot fully account for what happened', Wammen told Berlingske. Parts of the investigation 'could have been handled differently, faster and better', he said.

copy.headline: South African jurist who pursued war crimes wins the Nobel Peace Prize

standard.text: Navi Pillay, an 85-year-old South African human rights lawyer, won the Nobel Peace Prize on Friday. The Norwegian Nobel Committee credited her with ensuring that war crimes, crimes against humanity and genocide are prosecuted.

Under apartheid she defended Nelson Mandela, who became South Africa's first black president. She was later a judge at the UN's war crimes tribunal for Rwanda and the International Criminal Court, and the UN's high commissioner for human rights. She now sits on the International Court of Justice, the UN's principal court.
A UN commission she chaired concluded last year that Israel was committing genocide in Gaza. Israel condemned the award.

short.text: Navi Pillay, an 85-year-old South African human rights lawyer, won the Nobel Peace Prize on Friday for her work to see war crimes, crimes against humanity and genocide prosecuted. A UN commission she chaired found last year that Israel was committing genocide in Gaza; Israel condemned the award.
